arXiv:2609.14057v1 [cs.CL] 12 Sep 2026

Measuring the Creativity of Frontier LLMs in Automated Research

Yiheng Zhao Affiliation: Concordia University, Montreal, Canada    Mengzhuo Chen Affiliation: Independent Researcher    Chengming Hu Affiliation: Mcgill University, Montreal, Canada    Pengyi Liao Affiliation: Concordia University, Montreal, Canada    Yiran Pang Affiliation: Florida Atlantic University, Boca Raton, USA Affiliation: Correspondence:ypang2022@fau.edu*Equal contribution
Abstract

Frontier LLMs are increasingly capable of conducting automated research, yet their creativity in this setting has not been systematically evaluated. In this paper, we propose a set of metrics to evaluate creativity along the two dimensions of valueness and novelty. Valueness assesses whether each proposed idea is useful, while novelty is evaluated from three perspectives: whether the same idea has appeared before (Exact-Match P-Novelty), whether a previously unexplored variable or variable combination is explored (Variable-level P-Novelty), and whether the idea directly follows retrieved external knowledge or departs from it (H-Novelty). Our evaluation shows that the models achieve relatively similar scores on most creativity metrics, but differ substantially in Variable-level P-Novelty, which reflects the breadth of research-space exploration. Further correlation and idea-level performance analyses show that Variable-level P-Novelty is the creativity dimension most strongly associated with research performance.

1 Introduction

Scientific research is inherently a long-horizon iterative process, involving idea generation, experimentation, evaluation, and analysis. Since the speed of this iterative process is constrained by human researchers, frontier LLM are increasingly shifting from assisting human researchers to directly conducting automated research (Karpathy, 2026; Novikov et al., 2025; Xu et al., 2026). Although these models are now capable of conducting automated research, an important question arises: how creative are they? This question is critical because idea generation is a central component of scientific research, and effective research requires not merely generating ideas, but generating ideas that are both novel and valuable. In cognitive science, novelty and valueness are regarded as the two necessary components of creativity (Boden, 2004).

However, existing work has not systematically evaluated their creativity in this setting. To address this gap, we propose a set of metrics that evaluate the creativity of LLM-based research agents along the two dimensions of valueness and novelty. Valueness assesses whether the idea proposed in each iteration is useful, while novelty assesses whether the idea proposed in each iteration is new under different novelty criteria. For novelty, we consider three criteria. The first determines whether the same idea has appeared in previous iterations, where two ideas are considered the same if they modify the same variable(s) to the same post-modification value(s). This criterion corresponds to Exact-Match P-Novelty. The second determines whether the variable or combination of variables modified in the current iteration has been explored before, regardless of the specific values assigned to them. This criterion corresponds to Variable-level P-Novelty. The third determines whether the model generates the proposed idea by directly following external knowledge retrieved. This criterion corresponds to H-Novelty.

Our evaluation shows that the models achieve relatively similar Valueness, Exact-Match P-Novelty, and H-Novelty scores, while exhibiting substantially larger differences in Variable-level P-Novelty, which reflects the breadth of research-space exploration. Through correlation analysis and further analysis of the performance gains associated with different types of ideas, we find that Variable-level P-Novelty is the creativity dimension most strongly associated with research performance.

2 Related Work

2.1 Automated Research Systems

Recent automated-research systems place agents in closed propose–execute–evaluate loops. Karpathy’s autoresearch provides a minimal instance, autonomously modifying and evaluating an LLM training program under fixed compute Karpathy (2026). AlphaEvolve combines LLM program generation with evolutionary search to discover both deployable optimizations and new algorithms Novikov et al. (2025), while Google’s AI co-scientist extends iterative search to scientific hypotheses, including proposals validated experimentally Gottweis et al. (2025). More recent results further demonstrate autonomous optimization and frontier mathematical discovery Recursive (2026); OpenAI (2026a); Anthropic (2026b).

2.2 Creativity and Research Idea Generation

Creativity requires both originality and effectiveness Runco and Jaeger (2012). In scientific ideation, LLM-generated research ideas have been rated as more novel than human-generated ideas, but slightly less feasible Si et al. (2025), while generative AI can improve individual creativity at the cost of collective diversity Doshi and Hauser (2024). Recent work further shows that analogical reasoning can mitigate mode collapse and improve novelty and diversity Shen et al. (2026). Beyond these empirical measures, a recent position paper argues that genuine scientific invention requires an abductive jump from observations to novel explanatory hypotheses, a capability not captured by induction or deduction alone Zahavy (2026).

3 Creativity Metrics

In this section, we first introduce how creativity is characterized in cognitive science, then describe the automated research setting considered in our evaluation, and finally present our proposed metrics for evaluating creativity in automated research based on this formulation.

3.1 Creativity: Novelty and Valueness

In cognitive science, creativity is commonly characterized by two jointly necessary components: novelty and valueness Boden (2004). Novelty refers to the extent to which an idea departs from existing knowledge or established patterns, whereas valueness concerns whether the idea is useful or valuable in the relevant context.

Novelty can be considered with respect to two different reference frames: whether an idea is novel relative to the previous ideas of the individual who generates it, or novel relative to the whole of human history. These two notions correspond to psychological novelty (P-novelty) and historical novelty (H-novelty), respectively.

3.2 Automated Research Setting

We consider an iterative automated research setting following the general autoresearch paradigm. The process starts from an initial research baseline. At each iteration, the agent proposes a research idea together with the corresponding code modification. The proposed modification is applied to the current baseline and then evaluated.

If the modification improves the current baseline, it is kept and incorporated into the baseline for subsequent iterations. Otherwise, it is discarded, and the previous baseline is retained. This process is repeated iteratively.

3.3 Metrics

Valueness. We define Valueness as the fraction of research iterations whose proposed modifications are kept:

V=1N​∑i=1Nvi,V=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}v_{i},

where vi∈{0,1}v_{i}\in\{0,1\}, with vi=1v_{i}=1 if the modification proposed at iteration ii is kept, and vi=0v_{i}=0 if it is discarded.

P-Novelty. We define P-Novelty as the fraction of novel ideas among all research iterations. For each iteration, the proposed idea is compared against all ideas proposed in the preceding iterations. Formally,

P=1N​∑i=1Nni,P=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}n_{i},

where ni∈{0,1}n_{i}\in\{0,1\} indicates whether the idea proposed at iteration ii is novel with respect to all preceding iterations, with ni=1n_{i}=1 if the idea is novel and ni=0n_{i}=0 if it repeats a previously proposed idea. We evaluate P-Novelty at two levels of granularity: Exact-Match P-Novelty and Variable-level P-Novelty.

For Exact-Match P-Novelty, we determine whether an idea is novel based on the variable(s) modified by the model and their post-modification values. Two modifications are considered the same if they modify the same variable(s) to the same value(s). The values before modification are not considered. We define

ni={1,Mi≠Mj,∀j<i,0,otherwise.n_{i}=\begin{cases}1,&M_{i}\neq M_{j},\ \forall j<i,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

Thus, an idea is considered novel if the same code modification has not appeared in any preceding iteration. For Variable-level P-Novelty, we use a coarser criterion and consider only the variable(s) being modified, regardless of their post-modification values.

H-Novelty. We define H-Novelty as the fraction of knowledge-departing ideas among all research iterations. For each iteration, we examine the reasoning trace and classify the proposed idea as either knowledge-following or knowledge-departing. In this paper, we define an idea as knowledge-following if the model explicitly states in its reasoning trace that a specific setting is used in an existing project, paper, repository, or other external reference, and consequently proposes a change that follows or aligns with that referenced knowledge. The proposed change does not need to exactly reproduce the referenced implementation, as long as it does not go beyond the conclusion supported by the referenced knowledge. Otherwise, the idea is considered knowledge-departing.

Formally,

H=1N​∑i=1Nhi,H=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}h_{i},

where hi∈{0,1}h_{i}\in\{0,1\}, with hi=1h_{i}=1 for a knowledge-departing idea and hi=0h_{i}=0 for a knowledge-following idea.

4 Experiments

4.1 Setup

Agent Setup. We use Codex CLI as the agent framework with six models: GLM-5.2 (Z.ai, 2026), Kimi K3 (Moonshot AI, 2026), Qwen3.7-Max (Qwen Team, 2026), Claude Opus 4.8 (Anthropic, 2026a), GPT-5.5 (OpenAI, 2026b), and DeepSeek V4 Pro (DeepSeek-AI, 2026). We enable thinking with max reasoning effort, using xhigh for GPT, and follow the developers’ recommended inference settings, referring to Hugging Face model cards where available.

Datasets. We adopt the research task and data provided by Karpathy’s autoresearch project (Karpathy, 2026), running each model for 100 iterations.

Experimental Hardware. All evaluations are conducted on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU.

4.2 Evaluation Method

We implement an automated evaluation to compute the proposed creativity metrics for each model. For Valueness, each iteration explicitly records whether the proposed modification is kept or discarded. We therefore compute this metric deterministically by exact matching against the recorded decisions. For the three novelty metrics, the evaluation tasks are sufficiently straightforward for current LLMs. We therefore design prompts based on the criteria for determining whether each iteration is novel and use GPT-5.6-Sol with high reasoning effort to perform the evaluation. We manually verify the resulting judgments to ensure their reliability. Because raw reasoning traces are unavailable for Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5, we do not evaluate H-Novelty for these two models.

4.3 Main Results

Table 1 presents the creativity evaluation results. Valueness varies relatively little across models, with GPT-5.5 achieving the highest score of 0.28 and the remaining models ranging from 0.22 to 0.24. Exact-Match P-Novelty is consistently high, ranging from 0.84 to 0.96, indicating that most proposed ideas differ from previous ones at the fine-grained intervention level. In contrast, Variable-level P-Novelty shows substantially greater variation across models, ranging from 0.22 to 0.48. Kimi K3 achieves the highest score (0.48), followed by Qwen3.7-Max (0.42), Claude Opus 4.8 (0.40), and GLM-5.2 (0.39), while GPT-5.5 has the lowest score (0.22). H-Novelty is also generally high among the four models for which it can be evaluated, ranging from 0.85 to 0.94, with DeepSeek V4 Pro achieving the highest score. Overall, the main difference across models lies in Variable-level P-Novelty, which reflects the breadth of research-space exploration.

4.4 Which Dimensions of Creativity Matter for Performance?

Figure 1 shows the running-best validation BPB over the 100 research iterations. To compare models fairly, we define final improvement as the common baseline BPB minus the final BPB, so larger values are better. Table 2 reports the model-level correlation between each creativity metric and final improvement.

To investigate which dimensions of creativity are important for research performance, we conduct a correlation analysis between each creativity metric and final improvement. Figure 1 compares the running-best validation BPB and final improvement across models over 100 research iterations. Table 2 reports the correlation results. From Table 2, we observe that Variable-level P-Novelty exhibits the strongest positive correlation with final improvement (r=0.788r=0.788), suggesting that the breadth of research-space exploration is closely associated with final improvement, with higher Variable-level P-Novelty corresponding to greater improvement.

To further support this finding, we categorize the proposed ideas according to their P-Novelty and analyze their contributions to performance improvement. Ideas with Variable-level P-Novelty account for 62.8% of the total improvement. Moreover, among successful ideas, their average BPB gain is approximately three times that of ideas that are Exact-Match novel but not Variable-level novel (0.001362 versus 0.000449). These results provide further evidence that exploring new regions of the research space is particularly important for achieving larger performance improvements.

5 Conclusion

In this work, we study the creativity of frontier LLMs in automated research by proposing metrics that characterize valueness and novelty under different criteria. Evaluating six models in Karpathy’s autoresearch project, we find that the models are relatively similar on most creativity metrics but differ substantially in Variable-level P-Novelty, which reflects the breadth of research-space exploration. Further analysis shows that this dimension is most strongly associated with research performance, suggesting that effective automated research depends not only on generating different ideas, but also on exploring new regions of the research space.
